text.title: Structured Logging Patterns Worked Example
text.summary: One end-to-end trace: a service with printf logs, no correlation and an unsampled hot loop, walked gate by gate to the artefact matching the output contract.

section.title: Trace
section.p: Audit of a Python backend finds 90 printf-style log calls (`logger.info(f"user {user.email} did {action}")`), no correlation id anywhere, four ad-hoc masking helpers, and one worker loop logging per iteration.

Gates in decision-tree order: plain-text logs block first, so step 1 installs the JSON renderer. Step 2 wires the middleware and the `contextvars` binding, and the Celery task base class is patched so child contexts inherit rather than starting a fresh id. Step 3 collapses the four masking helpers into one processor and adds the value-level regexes — the email inside the f-string was invisible to field-name masking, which is why the leak survived three reviews. Step 4 reclassifies 12 calls from ERROR to WARN. Step 5 adds the three perf fields at egress. Step 6 finds the worker loop at 4,000 lines/s against a 200 lines/s budget and replaces it with a per-batch aggregate.

example.code: logger.info(f"user {user.email} did {action}") # PII in the message, nothing queryable print("here") # escapes redaction and correlation entirely
example.note: Neither line carries a correlation id, and the first one puts an email address in the sink for its whole retention period.
The email is absent by construction rather than by masking, and every field is queryable in the aggregator.
`redaction_pipeline_count` is exactly 1 — the schema caps it at 1 deliberately, because two pipelines is the shape that drifts.
